title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Assessment of gestational age by sonography addresses a fundamental clinical problem in obstetric care: inaccurate dating of pregnancy, which may result from uncertain last menstrual period, irregular menstrual cycles, recent hormonal contraception, the use of assisted reproductive techniques, or delayed presentation to care. Imprecise gestational dating is associated with inappropriate timing of antenatal surveillance, misinterpretation of fetal growth, suboptimal management of preterm or postterm pregnancy, and avoidable maternal or neonatal morbidity. Patients commonly present with indications for sonographic dating during early prenatal visits, evaluation of uterine size–date discrepancy, and assessment of threatened pregnancy complications, or prior to obstetric interventions.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Obstetric sonography estimates gestational age through standardized biometric measurements, providing an objective and reproducible framework for pregnancy dating. Indications include uncertain clinical dating, high-risk pregnancy, and planning of obstetric management, whereas contraindications are limited and primarily relate to patient instability or inability to obtain adequate images. Technical challenges include poor acoustic windows, fetal position, and advanced gestational age. Failure to perform accurate sonographic dating may lead to gestational age misclassification, inappropriate intervention, or delayed recognition of fetal compromise. Procedural risks are minimal when performed correctly.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to sharpen learners’ skills in integrating sonographic gestational age assessment into obstetric risk stratification and management. Participants will gain deeper insights into the procedure's diagnostic role, indications, contraindications, equipment and preparation requirements, and proper technique. Enhanced proficiency will facilitate clinician participation in interprofessional efforts addressing the needs of patients with uncomplicated and high-risk pregnancies.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify patients presenting for prenatal care who require sonographic evaluation to support accurate gestational dating, risk stratification, and appropriate clinical intervention. Implement the recommended sonographic techniques for fetal dating, including appropriate probe selection, image orientation, and biometric measurement, to support clinical decision-making. Improve patient understanding of the purpose, process, and limitations of sonographic gestational age assessment to enhance cooperation and support optimal prenatal care outcomes. Collaborate with other healthcare professionals, including maternal-fetal medicine specialists, pediatricians, and obstetricians, to manage both routine and high-risk pregnancies and coordinate a comprehensive obstetric care plan. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Introduction
content: Recent studies continue to support 1st-trimester ultrasonography as the most reliable method for determining gestational age while also refining measurement interpretation. New crown-rump length (CRL) dating formulas derived from pregnancies with known conception dates demonstrate improved precision compared with older reference equations, with most estimates falling within 0 to 2 days of the true gestational age (see Image . Crown-Rump Length Measurement). [1] Recently published early pregnancy reference charts based on accurately dated pregnancies, including assisted reproductive technology cohorts, suggest that traditional curves based on the last menstrual period (LMP) may slightly overestimate gestational age at the extremes of early development, supporting the use of updated population-specific charts. [2]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Introduction
content: Beyond improvements in biometric standards, advances in ultrasound technology have expanded the role of point-of-care imaging. Studies evaluating artificial intelligence–assisted and portable ultrasound devices show gestational age estimates obtained by novice users are comparable to those generated by experienced sonographers using high-end machines, particularly in the 2nd trimester. [3] Deep learning-based approaches further demonstrate the ability to estimate gestational age with mean errors of only a few days across multiple trimesters, sometimes outperforming conventional biometric methods. [4]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Introduction
content: Measurement of CRL on the 1st-trimester ultrasound between 8 weeks 0 days and 13 weeks 6 days is the most accurate approach to gestational age dating and is the gold standard for pregnancy assessment. Recent findings suggest that updated reference data and emerging artificial intelligence-supported technologies may further improve accuracy, consistency, and access to reliable gestational age evaluation across diverse clinical settings.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Three structures are sequentially identifiable on a 1st-trimester ultrasound: the gestational sac, the yolk sac, and the embryonic pole. The gestational sac appears at approximately 5 weeks of gestation (30 days after LMP) and represents the chorionic sac. The gestational sac presents as a small hypoechoic structure near the uterine fundus and grows approximately 1 mm per day after visualization (see Image . Gestational Sac Measurement). The yolk sac appears as a round echogenic ring with a hypoechoic center at approximately 5.5 weeks but is unreliable and, therefore, not used to determine gestational age.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The embryonic pole appears at approximately 6 weeks. [5] This structure initially presents as a small linear formation congruent with the yolk sac, giving the appearance of a signet ring. The embryonic pole is the first feature measurable to obtain CRL, providing an accurate estimate of gestational age.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The embryonic pole develops cephalic and caudal portions, which are initially tightly wrapped around the embryo. The first true CRL measurements may be obtained as these structures unfold and limb buds appear. Differentiation between embryo and fetus occurs at approximately 9 weeks, when organogenesis completes, and growth focuses on maturation of existing structures. [6]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Indications
content: Sonographic determination of gestational age is indicated in any pregnant individual with an unknown LMP to confirm estimated dates. This assessment tool is also recommended for patients with otherwise unknown gestational age.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Contraindications
content: Sonographic determination of gestational age has no known contraindications. Practitioners should apply the minimum ultrasonic energy necessary for the shortest duration required to obtain accurate measurements.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Equipment
content: Per current guidelines, the choice of probe in early pregnancy depends on image quality, clinical need, and patient factors rather than gestational age alone. A transvaginal probe may be recommended when transabdominal imaging is not definitive, and vice versa. [7] [8]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Equipment
content: Transvaginal or endocavitary probes are preferred when transabdominal imaging is suboptimal, particularly before 12 weeks of gestation or when an anomaly is suspected. Higher-frequency probes provide superior resolution and enhance detection rates of structural malformations. [9]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Equipment
content: Transabdominal probes, typically curvilinear and low-frequency, generally provide sufficient penetration and adequate resolution in most patients. Evidence demonstrates that for late 1st-trimester examinations (12–13 weeks), higher-frequency transabdominal probes (>5 MHz) successfully visualize fetal anatomy. A combined transabdominal and transvaginal approach optimizes detection of anomalies during this period. Studies show that this approach identifies more than half of all anomalies and nearly all severe abnormalities on early scans. [10]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Preparation
content: General and routine cleaning and maintenance of probes should follow the manufacturer's recommended instructions for use. Optimal images are obtained with the patient in a supine position when using the curvilinear probe and in the lithotomy position when using the endocavitary probe. For transabdominal examinations, the patient should have a full bladder or not have voided recently to utilize the urine-filled bladder as an echogenic window. A small amount of gel should be applied to the curvilinear probe, and the abdominopelvic region should be scanned in longitudinal and short axes.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Preparation
content: For transvaginal examinations, the patient should empty the bladder just prior to the exam, as the cervix provides an appropriate acoustic window. A full bladder may displace uterine anatomy, making detection and measurement of pregnancy difficult. The endocavitary probe is prepared by applying a small amount of ultrasound gel to the tip, covering the probe with a gel-lined probe cover, and optionally applying additional gel over the cover before placement in the vaginal vault.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment
content: Images of the developing fetus within the uterus are obtainable in transverse and sagittal planes using both curvilinear and endocavitary probes. Once the gestation is identified and images acquired, gestational age may be determined using LMP-based estimates or physical examination findings.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- First Trimester
content: The most accurate period to determine gestational age occurs in the 1st trimester, specifically between 8 and 12 weeks. [11] This timeframe corresponds to the period of fastest and most consistent embryonic growth, allowing gestational age estimation with an accuracy of approximately 5 days. [12]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- First Trimester
content: The gestational sac is first visualized at approximately 5 weeks on transvaginal examination and 6 weeks on transabdominal examination. The sac grows approximately 1 mm per day. [13] Recent guidelines recommend against using the mean sac diameter for estimating due dates, as accuracy declines once the sac exceeds 14 mm.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- First Trimester
content: Embryonic gestational age is determined by measuring the mean sac diameter from inside wall to inside wall. Three orthogonal measurements using sagittal and transverse views may be obtained if the gestational sac is irregular. The mean sac diameter is then compared with reference tables, entered into regression models, or input into the ultrasound machine to calculate estimated gestational age using preset obstetric settings. [14] [15]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- First Trimester
content: Of 1st-trimester methods, CRL provides the most accurate determination of gestational age. CRL is first measurable at approximately 6 weeks when the embryo appears adjacent to the yolk sac as a linear hyperechoic structure. Accuracy is highest from 6 to 10 weeks during the period of most rapid and consistent growth. CRL may be measured up to approximately 14 weeks, with an accuracy of 3 to 8 days. [16] Measurement is taken from the outermost cephalic portion to the rump, excluding limbs and the yolk sac. Most ultrasound machines calculate gestational age based on these measurements. Published reference tables or regression models can provide accurate estimates when automated calculation is unavailable. [17] [18]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- Second Trimester
content: Second-trimester dating relies on composite fetal measurements rather than individual parameters. According to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), gestational age assessment from 14 weeks to 21 weeks 6 days is based on a combination of fetal biometry, including biparietal diameter, head circumference, femur length, and abdominal circumference, with a margin of error of 7 to 10 days (see Image . Fetal Biparietal Diameter and Head Circumference in the Second Trimester). Between 22 weeks and 27 weeks 6 days, accuracy decreases to a margin of error of 10 to 14 days.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- Second Trimester
content: Recent evidence favors multiparameter models over single-parameter approaches. A 2024 validation study comparing 189 equations demonstrated that multiparameter models consistently provided more accurate gestational age estimates, whereas models based solely on head circumference showed higher error rates. [19]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- Second Trimester
content: Technical aspects of measurement follow the current practice parameters of the American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine (AIUM), American College of Radiology (ACR), ACOG, Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM), and Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound (SRU). Biparietal diameter is measured from outer to inner calvarial edges. Head circumference is measured along the outer perimeter of the calvarium. Abdominal circumference is measured at the level of the portal vein bifurcation with the stomach visible (see Image . Fetal Abdominal Circumference). Femur length is measured perpendicular to the shaft while excluding cartilage (see Image . Fetal Femur Measurement).

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- Third Trimester
content: The ACOG notes that the 3rd-trimester ultrasound (>28 weeks) is the least reliable method for determining gestational age, with a margin of error of 21 to 30 days. Third-trimester biometric measurements should not be used alone to establish or revise gestational age. Relying solely on 3rd-trimester ultrasound can be misleading, as apparent discrepancies may reflect pathologic fetal growth restriction rather than errors in earlier gestational dating. Best practice is to adjust the estimated due date only if the 1st ultrasound is performed in the 3rd trimester and shows a discrepancy greater than 21 days. [20]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Technique or Treatment -- Third Trimester
content: Even in this scenario, the overall clinical picture should guide the decision, often requiring careful follow-up and repeat ultrasounds to monitor interval growth. This cautious approach is taken because gestational dating is more accurate in the 1st and early 2nd trimesters (margin of error 5 to 7 days in the 1st trimester; margin of error 7 to 10 days in the early 2nd trimester). When a pregnancy has already been dated by an earlier, more reliable ultrasound assessment, size discrepancies in the 3rd trimester should prompt evaluation for growth abnormalities rather than automatic redating.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Complications
content: Ultrasound during pregnancy is considered safe when used appropriately for clinical purposes, with no documented adverse effects on the fetus. The ACOG recommends that diagnostic ultrasound be performed when clinically indicated and in accordance with the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle to minimize fetal exposure.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Complications
content: Accurate determination of gestational age is essential for clinical decision-making, particularly in late-term and postterm pregnancies. First-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL provides the most precise estimation of gestational age. The reliability of ultrasound dating declines as pregnancy progresses, with 2nd- and 3rd-trimester measurements associated with increasing margins of error, with a margin of error of at least 2 weeks in late pregnancy. [21] Inaccurate gestational dating may result in inappropriate clinical management, including unnecessary labor induction or delayed identification of fetal growth abnormalities.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Complications
content: The concept of the pseudogestational sac is now considered outdated and lacks clinical relevance with modern ultrasound technology. In a study of 649 women with pregnancies of unknown location, all intrauterine fluid collections were confirmed as true gestational sacs, with no cases of pseudogestational sacs identified. [22]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Complications
content: When an intrauterine fluid collection is visualized in the absence of an extraovarian adnexal mass, the likelihood that it represents an intrauterine gestational sac exceeds 99.5%. This observation significantly reduces the probability of misdiagnosing an ectopic pregnancy in early gestation.

content: Intrauterine fluid collections were observed in 4.9% of ectopic pregnancies compared with 46% of intrauterine pregnancies. The presence of such a collection was associated with a low ectopic pregnancy rate of 2.2%. [23]

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Clinical Significance
content: Accurate dating is essential for guiding obstetric care, including timing and interpretation of antepartum testing, assessment of fetal growth, and planning interventions to prevent preterm births, postterm births, and related morbidities. [24] Determination of fetal viability relies on precise assessment of gestational age, with 1st-trimester ultrasound measurement of CRL providing the most accurate dating, with a margin of error of 5 to 7 days. This level of accuracy is particularly important when making decisions regarding life-saving interventions during the periviable period.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Clinical Significance
content: Decisions regarding delivery timing and mode of delivery are highly dependent on accurate gestational dating. A study demonstrated a reduced need for postterm labor induction among women who underwent routine 1st-trimester ultrasound compared with those who received only 2nd-trimester ultrasounds.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Clinical Significance
content: Accurate gestational dating is also critical for assessing fetal growth and evaluating whether biometric measurements correspond to gestational age. Discrepancies between expected gestational age and fetal measurements may indicate growth abnormalities. Establishing accurate dating early is critical for reliable growth monitoring later in gestation since ultrasound dating accuracy declines in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, with a margin of error of at least 2 weeks in late pregnancy.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Gestational age is most accurately established during the 1st trimester, particularly around 7 weeks of gestation. Measurements should be clearly documented and communicated to all members of the interprofessional healthcare team. Accurate documentation ensures continuity of care and supports appropriate clinical decision-making as the pregnancy progresses, ultimately optimizing outcomes for both mother and fetus.

title: Sonography Assessment of Gestational Age -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Point-of-care ultrasound is frequently used to determine gestational age. Best practice includes transmitting ultrasound images to the patient’s medical record along with a detailed procedural note describing the findings. Sonographic features observed during gestational sac evaluation that raise concern for a pseudogestational sac require further investigation to exclude ectopic pregnancy, which can be life-threatening. Effective communication and coordination among interprofessional team members ensure timely follow-up and emergent consultation when an ectopic pregnancy is suspected.
